title: Graphs and honest scales

prerequisite.prompt: Counts are 8 and 10. What is their absolute difference?

vocabulary: A reference line with a scale on a graph
The starting reference value on a scale
A graph using bar lengths to compare categories
The mapping from values to positions or lengths

blocks.text: A fictional poll records 8 votes for Drawing and 10 for Building. A bar chart should make lengths proportional to counts, starting at zero. A chart starting at 7 makes the visible bars 1 and 3 units tall and can exaggerate the difference.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
Follow the evidence
blocks.caption: Read each row from left to right and connect the evidence to the stated rule.

blocks.text: The text chart uses one # per vote and a zero baseline. The second category has 2 more votes and 1.25 times as many votes, not three times as many. Include the poll question, date or collection occasion and number of responses when presenting a real graph.

blocks.label: Draw bars for counts 4 and 6 using one square per vote. State the difference and ratio.

blocks.text: A graph with bars beginning at 7 turns counts 8 and 10 into visible lengths 1 and 3. Redraw from zero and label counts directly. A line chart can use a restricted axis for detail if clearly labelled, but it must not disguise its scale.

Counts alone do not show why students chose an activity or whether nonrespondents would choose differently. Graph choices should match the question: categories suit bars; ordered time observations can suit a line.

workbook.title: Read the scale
workbook.prompt: A bar is 6 squares long with 2 votes per square. How many votes is that?

workbook.title: Compare fairly
workbook.prompt: Counts are 12 and 15. State the difference and ratio using the true values.

workbook.title: Repair a misleading graph
workbook.prompt: Bars for 12 and 15 start at 10. Explain the misleading lengths and repair.
workbook.answer: Visible lengths 2 and 5 suggest a 2.5 ratio. Start at zero, use a common scale and label counts 12 and 15.

workbook.title: Draw independently
workbook.prompt: Draw a bar chart for Music 6, Art 9, Coding 3. Include title, category labels, vote units, zero baseline and equal scale. State two supported comparisons.
workbook.answer: Music 6, Art 9, Coding 3 on one scale. Art has 3 more than Music and three times Coding. Accept other correct comparisons.

workbook.title: Limit the claim
workbook.prompt: Art has the most votes among 18 responses. Does that establish Art is best for learning?
workbook.answer: No. Preference counts do not measure learning effectiveness or establish a cause.

teacher.background: Teach Week 18 as a two-session investigation using fictional data. A fictional poll records 8 votes for Drawing and 10 for Building. A bar chart should make lengths proportional to counts, starting at zero. A chart starting at 7 makes the visible bars 1 and 3 units tall and can exaggerate the difference. Assess the three stated outcomes through the independent task, not by copying the worked result.

Paper trace table and the student workbook

sessions: Retrieve the prerequisite and explain the purpose in the opening section.
Read the worked example and diagram; ask learners to trace each step aloud.
Complete W1 and W2, then compare predictions with observed results.
Collect the guided prediction before running; discuss a mismatch and its cause.
Retrieve the main rule without showing the previous answer.
Use W3 to diagnose and repair the stated failure; rerun an earlier case.
Collect W4 independently, including code or plan, predictions and explanations, before hints.
Discuss W5 and the exit; use the fresh retry when support was needed.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Difference 2 votes; ratio 6/4 = 1.5. Both bars begin at zero. Exit: No. Preference counts do not measure learning effectiveness or establish a cause.
misconceptions: A successful run proves the conclusion

teacher.support: Use graph paper with a marked zero. Extension: show the same values on two clearly labelled scales and discuss visual emphasis.
